_doc: Per-ingredient decision depth for the menu-pricing study/ecosystem. Sourced + adversarially fact-checked culinary yields (cooked/juice/freeze/cut-spec), substitutes with a price-hedge verdict computed from our own co-movement data, trim-to-value, shelf-life/storage, and peak-quality season. Reference/book values — verify your own. Nulls = a value that could not be corroborated (dropped, never guessed).

acorn-squash.cutSpec: Seeded and peeled to raw flesh (US Foods 74%); deep ridges make hand-peeling wasteful, so practical yield can run lower.
acorn-squash.yieldSource: US Foods Common Product Yields (acorn flesh, raw 74%) — confirmed via search. Freeze: NCHFP (cook/mash, then freeze).
acorn-squash.yieldNote: US Foods puts acorn raw flesh near 0.74, but the ridges make hand-peeling wasteful — roast and scoop, or serve it in the half-shell, to skip the peel loss.

substitutes.name: butternut squash
substitutes.worksFor: soups, roasts, purees (sweeter, easier to peel)
substitutes.failsFor: acorn's natural bowl shape for stuffing and baking halves

substitutes.name: delicata squash
substitutes.worksFor: roasting rings (edible skin), stuffing
substitutes.failsFor: large-portion needs; delicata is smaller and stores shorter

acorn-squash.storageMethod: Store WHOLE in a cool, dry, dark spot ~50-55F for 1-2 months; do NOT refrigerate whole or store near apples/tomatoes (ethylene shortens life) — cut pieces refrigerate ~5 days.
acorn-squash.depthSource: University extension winter-squash storage guides (acorn whole 1-2 months; cut ~5 days refrigerated); USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
acorn-squash.depthNote: Acorn keeps 1-2 months (shorter than butternut) — its ridged bowl shape earns its keep as an edible vessel for stuffed plates.

apple.yieldSource: US Foods and Book of Yields both list apple peeled & cored at 76% (adjusted from 0.78, which no source supported); USDA FoodData Central refuse 10% skin-on (edible ~0.90); NCHFP frozen-fruit 8-12 mo.
apple.yieldNote: Peeling-and-coring costs ~24% (usable ~0.76); leave the skin on (cored only, ~0.90) wherever the recipe allows and you claw most of that waste back.

substitutes.name: firm pear (Bosc/Anjou)
substitutes.worksFor: pies, crisps, tarts, sauces, and slaws
substitutes.failsFor: when you need apple tartness or maximum hold-its-shape structure

substitutes.name: Asian pear
substitutes.worksFor: raw salads and slaws for crisp, juicy crunch
substitutes.failsFor: long bakes (breaks down softer) and applesauce-style body

apple.trimToValue: peels + cores -> scrap-apple vinegar or pectin-rich jelly; simmer for cider or stock
apple.storageMethod: Refrigerate in the crisper 32-36F (4-6 weeks, far beyond the counter); keep apples AWAY from ethylene-sensitive greens/herbs, and don't store bruised ones in the pile.
apple.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS): apples refrigerated 4-6 weeks; USDA SNAP-Ed + Cooperative Extension — US harvest Aug-Nov, cold/controlled-atmosphere storage keeps them available year-round.
apple.depthNote: Cold storage is an apple's superpower — crisper-held apples outlast the counter by weeks; just keep them away from your greens and herbs.

artichoke.cutSpec: Whole globe; edible = heart + tender leaf bases (USDA ~60% refuse). Trimmed to hearts-only is ~0.25.
artichoke.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse 60% (artichokes, globe, raw) — confirmed via search; hearts-only trim ~0.25. Freeze: NCHFP (blanched hearts in acidulated water).
artichoke.yieldNote: 60% of a whole globe is inedible — cost artichoke dishes by the heart, and buy trimmed or frozen hearts whenever the labor plus waste beats the premium.

substitutes.name: canned/jarred/frozen artichoke hearts
substitutes.worksFor: dips, pastas, pizza, salads, antipasto
substitutes.failsFor: whole steamed-artichoke service where guests pull the leaves

substitutes.name: hearts of palm
substitutes.worksFor: salads and antipasto for similar tender texture
substitutes.failsFor: artichoke's nutty flavor and hot dips

artichoke.trimToValue: peel the stalk -> it's an edible extension of the heart; cook it alongside
artichoke.storageMethod: Refrigerate unwashed in a bag, misted lightly to prevent drying, ~32-40F; do NOT store dry and uncovered (petals dry and brown) — a splash of water on the cut stem helps.
artichoke.peakSeason: spring, peak April-May (smaller second crop in fall)
artichoke.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS), whole fresh artichokes 1-2 weeks refrigerated; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
artichoke.depthNote: Bagged and lightly misted, whole artichokes hold about a week — buy fresh whole ones for spring specials and keep jarred hearts for the standing pasta or dip.

arugula.cutSpec: Cello/bagged baby arugula, trimmed. Bunched arugula with stems runs ~0.85 after trimming stem ends.
arugula.yieldSource: Foodservice produce-yield charts (Chefs-Resources / trade): cleaned/bagged arugula ~0.95-0.99 usable, loss only from trimming brown stem ends.
arugula.yieldNote: Cello/baby arugula is near-zero waste, so only pay a bunch premium if the price gap beats the ~10-15% stem loss on bunched.

substitutes.name: watercress
substitutes.worksFor: peppery salads, sandwich/garnish accents, the same mustard bite
substitutes.failsFor: bulk salad volume — watercress is delicate and pricier per usable ounce

substitutes.name: baby spinach
substitutes.worksFor: salad volume and a milder base when you want the green without the heat
substitutes.failsFor: dishes built on arugula's pepper — spinach reads flat where the bite is the point

substitutes.name: mizuna or baby mustard greens
substitutes.worksFor: peppery salad mixes and quick wilts
substitutes.failsFor: wide DMV availability — often a specialty-order item, not always on the truck

arugula.trimToValue: wilting/past-prime arugula -> arugula pesto same-day, or wilt into pasta, pizza, or soup
arugula.storageMethod: Refrigerate cold in its clamshell with a paper towel; do NOT wash until use — this is your most perishable green, so hold it dry and use it fast.
arugula.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper/FoodSafety.gov (tender greens ~3-5 days refrigerated) + USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide and Oklahoma State Extension (cool-season, bolts/turns bitter in summer heat).
arugula.depthNote: Treat it like an herb, not a lettuce — buy small, use in 2-3 days, and turn any turning batch into pesto the same day.

asparagus.cutSpec: Woody ends removed down to the tender spear (USDA ~47% refuse); snapping only the very base yields ~0.80.
asparagus.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse ~47% (asparagus, raw) → 0.53 for full woody-end trim; US Foods ~80% reflects snapping only the base. Freeze: NCHFP blanched 8–12 mo at 0°F.
asparagus.yieldNote: Standard asparagus loses nearly half to woody ends — buy thicker grades billed by the trimmed spear, or peel the lower stalk to reclaim yield before you pay for waste.

substitutes.name: green beans
substitutes.worksFor: blanched, sauteed or roasted green side
substitutes.failsFor: grilled whole spears or shaved-raw asparagus salad

substitutes.name: broccolini
substitutes.worksFor: grilled or roasted spears, hollandaise pairings
substitutes.failsFor: the distinct grassy asparagus flavor in a featured spring dish

asparagus.trimToValue: woody snapped ends -> simmer, then blend and strain for asparagus stock or soup base
asparagus.storageMethod: Refrigerate upright with cut ends in ~1 inch of water (or wrap ends in a damp towel), ~32-36F; do NOT store dry, sealed, or at room temp — spears toughen and dry within a day.
asparagus.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS), asparagus 3-4 days refrigerated; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
asparagus.depthNote: It only holds 3-4 days and toughens by the hour — buy asparagus for a dated spring feature, not as a standing line item.

banana.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central banana refuse 36% (edible 0.64) + US Foods flesh raw 66% — 0.65 central; USDA FoodKeeper frozen bananas ~2-3 mo.
banana.yieldNote: A third of every banana is peel, so price banana dishes off ~65% usable; freeze over-ripes peeled (~3 mo) for bread and smoothies instead of tossing them.

substitutes.name: unsweetened applesauce (baking binder)
substitutes.worksFor: replacing banana's moisture and binding in quick breads and muffins
substitutes.failsFor: banana flavor itself (nothing replaces it) and fresh eating

substitutes.name: very ripe plantain (cooked)
substitutes.worksFor: cooked and fried sweet applications
substitutes.failsFor: raw eating and delicate banana desserts; must be cooked

banana.trimToValue: overripe/blackened bananas -> peel and freeze for banana bread or smoothies; peels -> compost
banana.storageMethod: Hold at room temp; NEVER refrigerate green/unripe bananas (chill injury blackens skin and stalls ripening); once ripe, fridge to buy 2-3 days or freeze for baking, and keep away from ethylene-sensitive produce.
banana.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS) + university extension: bananas are a room-temp staple (refrigerate only once ripe), so a fresh-hold day count is not the planning metric (days = null); imported year-round.
banana.depthNote: Green in, room temp to ripen, and freeze the blackened ones for bread — never fridge unripe bananas or they'll blacken without ever sweetening.

basil.yieldSource: Chefs Resources / NPC produce-yield chart: basil 56% edible (stemless leaf per bunch), corroborated via search. Not citrus (juice null); raw finish (cooked null); leaves blacken on freezing and no authoritative 0F quality figure exists (freeze null).
basil.yieldNote: Whole plated leaves waste almost nothing, but picking leaves for pesto or chiffonade strips off ~44% as stem, so price those preps at AP cost divided by about 0.56 (roughly 1.8x).

substitutes.name: fresh mint
substitutes.worksFor: Thai/Vietnamese dishes, salads, and garnish where you want a bright top-note
substitutes.failsFor: classic pesto and Caprese, where sweet basil's anise character defines the dish

substitutes.name: fresh oregano or marjoram
substitutes.worksFor: cooked tomato sauces, pizza, and braises
substitutes.failsFor: raw uses like pesto or Caprese where basil's sweetness has to read

substitutes.name: flat-leaf parsley (as a pesto base)
substitutes.ratio: 1:1 by volume for the green base
substitutes.worksFor: green sauces/pesto where you want body and color and can add other aromatics
substitutes.failsFor: recreating basil's specific anise aroma on its own

basil.trimToValue: basil stems -> blend into pesto or steep into infused oil/simple syrup
basil.storageMethod: Hold at cool room temp (~55-60F), stems standing in water like cut flowers, loosely tented; do NOT refrigerate — cold below ~50F causes chilling injury that blackens the leaves.
basil.depthSource: UC Davis Postharvest Center (fresh culinary herbs, chilling sensitivity) and PMC review of basil shelf life (marketable room-temp life ~7 days; chilling injury below ~50F); Penn State Extension and Old Farmer's Almanac confirm summer field peak
basil.depthNote: Buy basil for the week you'll use it and hold it like cut flowers on the line, not in the walk-in — cold is what turns your garnish black.

beef-tenderloin.cutSpec: Peeled tenderloin, chain & silverskin removed (light trim); a whole PSMO/untrimmed piece drops usable to ~0.52-0.70
beef-tenderloin.yieldSource: US Foods / NAMP fabrication yields (peeled-from-PSMO ~52%; already-peeled further-trim ~0.85); USDA Nutrient Data Set for Retail Beef Cuts cooking reference (0.74-0.75); USDA/FSIS FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart (fresh beef 4-12 mo).
beef-tenderloin.yieldNote: Its cost lives in the trim: the 0.85 yield only holds for an already-peeled piece, so buy peeled and weigh usable meat before pricing, or a whole PSMO's ~0.52-0.70 will blow up the food cost you set.

substitutes.name: teres major (shoulder tender / petite tender)
substitutes.worksFor: tender medallions and steak plates at a fraction of the cost
substitutes.failsFor: a whole-roast Wellington presentation — it's a small single muscle

substitutes.name: top sirloin
substitutes.worksFor: medallions, skewers, and portioned steaks
substitutes.failsFor: the fork-tender, buttery texture filet is prized for

beef-tenderloin.trimToValue: the trimmed 'chain' muscle and silverskin-trimmed ends -> grind for tartare or burgers; head/tail tips -> stroganoff or skewers
beef-tenderloin.storageMethod: Refrigerate at 40F or below (ideally 32-36F) on the bottom shelf in a drip tray, wrapped; do NOT store above ready-to-eat foods, and do NOT leave out over 2 hours.
beef-tenderloin.peakSeason: year-round (US commodity beef holds consistent quality all year)
beef-tenderloin.depthSource: USDA FSIS 'Beef From Farm to Table' / AskUSDA 'Suggested storage times for beef' — fresh beef roasts & steaks 3-5 days refrigerated at <=40F; corroborated by FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart, FDA Refrigerator & Freezer Storage Chart, and Clemson HGIC 'Safe Handling of Beef'
beef-tenderloin.depthNote: Break down whole tenderloins in-house — the chain and tips become tartare, stroganoff, or skewers instead of paying for pre-cut filets.

beet.yieldSource: The Book of Yields topped-beet ~0.76 and US Foods 91% (already-topped, peeled & diced) bracket 0.75, which also absorbs topping loss; freezer 8-12 mo blanched (NCHFP/extension).
beet.yieldNote: Topped beets peel to ~75%; buy them topped (not bunched with greens) and roast whole to slip skins, losing less than raw peeling.
beet.trimToValue: beet greens -> saute like chard/spinach; peels -> stock or natural dye
beet.storageMethod: Refrigerate roots in a bag in the crisper; remove the greens (they pull moisture from the root) but keep them to cook — do NOT wash roots until use.
beet.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper / SDSU Extension, Storage Life of Vegetables (beet roots ~2 weeks refrigerated, months in cold storage); USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide
beet.depthNote: You bought the greens too — cook beet tops like chard instead of trashing them, and the case does double duty.

bell-pepper.cutSpec: Cored, seeded, stem and ribs removed (USDA sweet-pepper 18% refuse).
bell-pepper.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse 18% (peppers, sweet, raw) + The Book of Yields ~0.75–0.82. Freeze: peppers freeze raw unblanched, cooked-use (NCHFP).
bell-pepper.yieldNote: Only ~18% is core and seed, so peppers cost out well — but roasting-and-peeling drops you to ~0.70, so price roasted-pepper items higher.

substitutes.name: poblano pepper
substitutes.worksFor: roasting, stuffing, fajitas — adds mild heat and more flavor
substitutes.failsFor: raw sweet crunch in salads or crudite platters

substitutes.name: cubanelle / Italian frying pepper
substitutes.worksFor: sauteing, frying, sandwiches, sofrito
substitutes.failsFor: thick-walled raw crunch and stuffed-pepper structure

bell-pepper.trimToValue: tops, cores and trim -> freeze for vegetable stock or blend into sofrito
bell-pepper.storageMethod: Refrigerate dry and unwashed in the crisper, ~40-45F; do NOT wash until use (surface moisture speeds soft spots and mold).
bell-pepper.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS), bell peppers 4-14 days refrigerated; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
bell-pepper.depthNote: Red and yellow bells are just green bells left to ripen — in peak season the color premium narrows, so spec the color you actually plate.

blueberry.cutSpec: stems and soft/moldy culls removed (a clean clamshell is effectively ~1.0)
blueberry.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central cultivated-blueberry refuse ~0 (edible ~1.0); 0.95 reflects normal culling of soft berries; NCHFP/USDA FoodKeeper berries ~12 mo (blueberries freeze excellently).
blueberry.yieldNote: Blueberries are almost all usable, so your only loss is culling soft berries; buy fresh-dated, hold cold, and freeze surplus (quality ~12 mo) rather than let it turn.

substitutes.name: blackberries
substitutes.worksFor: sauces, compotes, pies, and mixed-berry bakes
substitutes.failsFor: muffins/pancakes where you want small berries that don't bleed color

substitutes.name: frozen blueberries
substitutes.worksFor: any cooked or baked use — sauces, muffins, compote
substitutes.failsFor: raw garnish and salads (thawed berries go soft and weep)

blueberry.trimToValue: soft/overripe berries -> compote, jam, or syrup; freeze surplus for baking
blueberry.storageMethod: Refrigerate unwashed and dry in a vented container (about 1-2 weeks); do NOT wash until use and do NOT seal airtight; sort out soft/moldy berries.
blueberry.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS): blueberries refrigerated 1-2 weeks; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide — US domestic Apr(GA/FL)-Sep, national peak Jun-Aug.
blueberry.depthNote: Blueberries are the sturdiest fresh berry (1-2 weeks cold) and freeze beautifully — a smart buy when a flat is priced to move.

bok-choy.cutSpec: Whole bok choy, root base trimmed (USDA FBG). Baby bok choy runs higher (~0.90+).
bok-choy.yieldSource: USDA FBG Section 2 (bok choy whole: 1 lb AP = 0.77 lb ready-to-serve, ~3.5 cups). Not sensibly frozen (very high water, goes limp) — freezeMonths null.
bok-choy.yieldNote: Only the root base trims off (~0.77 usable), and baby bok choy is nearly all usable — good for plate presence and low waste.

substitutes.name: napa cabbage
substitutes.worksFor: stir-fries, soups, and braises with similar mild sweetness
substitutes.failsFor: dishes built on bok choy's crisp white ribs — napa is softer and ruffled, not crunchy-stemmed

substitutes.name: Swiss chard (stems and leaves)
substitutes.worksFor: stir-fries and braises where you want a stem/leaf contrast
substitutes.failsFor: delicate Asian preparations — chard reads earthier and its color can bleed

substitutes.name: green cabbage
substitutes.worksFor: stir-fry crunch and volume
substitutes.failsFor: quick-cooking dishes — cabbage is firmer and needs longer than bok choy's fast-wilting leaves

bok-choy.trimToValue: root base and tough stem ends -> vegetable/stir-fry stock (leafy tops always stay usable)
bok-choy.storageMethod: Refrigerate unwashed in a perforated bag with a lightly damp paper towel; do NOT wash until use — it wants some humidity but rots if held wet.
bok-choy.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper/FoodSafety.gov and storage refs (tender brassica ~3-7 days, up to a week; yellows within a week) + extension cool-season guides (spring/fall, bolts in summer heat).
bok-choy.depthNote: One vegetable, two textures — crisp ribs and quick-wilting leaves; separate them and it drops into any stir-fry or soup.

broccoli.cutSpec: Whole bunch trimmed to florets + peeled tender stalk; leaves and woody base discarded (USDA ~39% refuse).
broccoli.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse 39% (broccoli, raw) — confirmed via search; corroborated by US Foods Common Product Yields (florets) and USDA FBG. Freeze: NCHFP blanched vegetables 8–12 mo at 0°F.
broccoli.yieldNote: A third of a crown is stalk and leaf — peel and use the stalk to claw back yield, or spec 'florets only' and cost the dish off ~0.47.

substitutes.name: cauliflower
substitutes.worksFor: roasting, gratins, soups, blanched sides, sheet-pan
substitutes.failsFor: dishes that need green color or crisp raw florets in slaw/crudite

substitutes.name: broccolini
substitutes.worksFor: sauteed or roasted green side, quick blanch
substitutes.failsFor: large-floret casseroles/gratins where mass and bite are wanted

broccoli.trimToValue: broccoli stalks -> peel and use for slaw, stir-fry, or simmer into soup/stock
broccoli.storageMethod: Refrigerate ~32-40F unwashed in a loose or perforated bag; do NOT wash until use or seal airtight (trapped moisture rots it), and keep away from apples (ethylene yellows the heads).
broccoli.peakSeason: fall (cool-season crop; lighter spring crop; California supplies much of the year)
broccoli.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS), broccoli 3-5 days refrigerated; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
broccoli.depthNote: You pay for florets but the peeled stalks slaw or soup for free — buy in the fall flush and stop trimming money into the bin.

brown-rice.yieldSource: USDA FBG Section 4 (Grains) and culinary references give ~3x dry-to-cooked (reported 2.5-4). StillTasty (FSIS-based) gives cooked brown rice 6 months best-quality frozen; The Kitchn/StillTasty document bran-oil rancidity shortening dry shelf life to ~3-6 months at room temp.
brown-rice.yieldNote: Brown rice sours in 3-6 months because its bran oil oxidizes, so buy only what you turn in a month or freeze the dry surplus to stop the clock -- then cost the ~3x cooked yield when you price the bowl (a cooked batch keeps ~6 months frozen).

substitutes.name: white rice
substitutes.worksFor: any pilaf, side, or bowl where cook speed and a soft grain are wanted
substitutes.failsFor: when you need brown rice's fiber, nutty flavor, and firmer chew

substitutes.name: quinoa
substitutes.worksFor: gluten-free bowls wanting more protein per portion
substitutes.failsFor: creamy/starchy rice roles like rice pudding, risotto, or sushi

substitutes.name: farro or barley
substitutes.worksFor: chewy whole-grain bowls and salads
substitutes.failsFor: gluten-free menus; longer cook time

brown-rice.trimToValue: day-old cooked brown rice -> fried rice, arancini, or rice pudding (drier chilled grains fry up separate instead of gummy)
brown-rice.storageMethod: Refrigerate cooked rice airtight at 40F or below within 2 hrs of cooking; store uncooked brown rice sealed in a cool dark pantry (its bran oils go rancid in ~6 months, unlike near-indefinite white rice) or fridge/freeze for long hold. Do NOT hold cooked rice warm or at room temp.
brown-rice.depthSource: USDA FSIS leftover guidance — cooked rice 3-4 days (https://ask.usda.gov/s/article/How-long-will-cooked-food-stay-safe-in-the-refrigerator); StillTasty brown-rice storage — bran oils turn rancid within ~6 months at room temp.
brown-rice.depthNote: Unlike white rice, brown rice's bran oils turn; buy it in tighter quantities and rotate the dry stock first.

brussels-sprouts.cutSpec: Loose sprouts, stem end and a few loose outer leaves trimmed.
brussels-sprouts.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse ~10% (brussels sprouts, raw) + US Foods Common Product Yields 90%. Freeze: NCHFP blanched vegetables 8–12 mo at 0°F.
brussels-sprouts.yieldNote: Loose sprouts run ~90% usable and cost out cleanly — only buy them on the stalk if it's cheaper per trimmed pound after the leaves fall off.

substitutes.name: shredded savoy or green cabbage
substitutes.worksFor: sauteed or roasted shreds, slaws, hash
substitutes.failsFor: whole-sprout roasting where you want individually caramelized halves

substitutes.name: broccoli florets
substitutes.worksFor: roasted vegetable side
substitutes.failsFor: shaved raw sprout salad

brussels-sprouts.trimToValue: loose outer leaves -> roast into crispy leaf 'chips'
brussels-sprouts.storageMethod: Refrigerate on the stalk if possible, or unwashed in a perforated bag at ~32F; do NOT wash or trim the bases until use (cut ends brown and soften fast).
brussels-sprouts.peakSeason: late fall to early winter — noticeably sweeter after the first frost
brussels-sprouts.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS), Brussels sprouts fresh 3-5 days refrigerated; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
brussels-sprouts.depthNote: Buy them on the stalk in late fall — they hold longer than loose sprouts and eat sweeter once frost has hit the field.

butter-lettuce.cutSpec: Whole butterhead/Boston head, root/core + loose outer leaves removed. Living (root-on) butter lettuce yields lower once the root ball is cut.
butter-lettuce.yieldSource: Culinary yield references for soft-head (butterhead/Boston/Bibb) lettuce, ~0.65-0.75 after removing core, root and bruised outer leaves. No direct USDA FBG line found (single-tier culinary reference only).
butter-lettuce.yieldNote: Living/root-on butterhead looks cheap by the head but loses its root ball and loose outer leaves — count on only ~0.70 usable.

substitutes.name: Bibb / Boston lettuce
substitutes.worksFor: lettuce cups, soft composed salads — same butterhead type, essentially interchangeable
substitutes.failsFor: nothing culinary; purely a naming/supply distinction within the butterhead family

substitutes.name: little gem / baby romaine
substitutes.worksFor: lettuce cups and single-serve salads with more structure
substitutes.failsFor: the signature loose, silky butterhead fold — gems are crisper and more upright

substitutes.name: green or red leaf lettuce
substitutes.worksFor: tender salads and sandwich layers
substitutes.failsFor: cupped applications — leaf lettuce won't hold a filling like a butterhead leaf

butter-lettuce.storageMethod: Refrigerate cold and unwashed; if sold live/rooted, keep the roots on and the base slightly moist; do NOT wash until use — the most fragile head lettuce, so use within days.
butter-lettuce.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper/FoodSafety.gov and grower storage refs (butterhead 5-7 days, shortest of the lettuces) + USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide (cool-season spring/fall field pattern).
butter-lettuce.depthNote: Buy live/rooted heads and keep the roots on — it's the difference between three days and a week of cup-worthy leaves.

butternut-squash.cutSpec: Peeled and seeded (USDA ~16% refuse → ~0.84 edible); heavy hand-peel loss can pull practical yield lower.
butternut-squash.yieldSource: USDA ~16% refuse / The Book of Yields ~0.84 (butternut) — confirmed via search; US Foods. Freeze: NCHFP blanched cubes or cooked purée.
butternut-squash.yieldNote: Butternut is one of the higher-yield winter squashes (~0.84 careful/machine peel) — weigh your hand-peel loss plus labor against pre-cut before paying the cut premium.

substitutes.name: kabocha or acorn squash
substitutes.worksFor: roasting, soups, purees
substitutes.failsFor: high-yield seedless neck prep — ridged squashes are harder to peel and cube cleanly

substitutes.name: sweet potato
substitutes.worksFor: soups, purees, roasting (sweeter)
substitutes.failsFor: savory, lower-sugar squash dishes wanting true squash flavor

butternut-squash.trimToValue: seeds -> roast like pepitas; peels -> crisp or add to stock
butternut-squash.storageMethod: Cure and store WHOLE in a cool, dry, dark spot ~50-55F for 2-3 months; do NOT refrigerate whole squash (cold shortens life) — once cut, wrap and refrigerate pieces ~5 days.
butternut-squash.peakSeason: fall through early winter (flavor sweetens weeks after harvest)
butternut-squash.depthSource: University extension winter-squash storage guides (whole 2-3 months cool/dry; cut ~5 days refrigerated); USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
butternut-squash.depthNote: Whole butternut is a 2-3 month pantry vegetable, not a walk-in item — buy deep at the fall harvest and store it dry and cool, never cold.

button-mushroom.yieldSource: US Foods 'Common Product Yields' chart (mushrooms 90% edible, corroborated via search); USDA Food Buying Guide (1 lb AP whole = 0.98 lb sliced and 0.43 lb cooked-drained, so ~0.44-0.45 cooked/raw); NCHFP Freezing Mushrooms (cook/blanch first) + extension blanched-vegetable freezer guidance (8-12 mo) support ~9 mo cook-first. Not citrus (juice null).
button-mushroom.yieldNote: Whole they're ~90% usable, but they cook down to under half their raw weight, so buy roughly 2 lb raw for every 1 lb you need cooked on the plate.

substitutes.name: cremini (baby bella)
substitutes.worksFor: any cooked or raw use — same species, slightly deeper flavor
substitutes.failsFor: dishes where you want a pale, white color in a cream or light sauce

button-mushroom.trimToValue: trimmed stem ends and stems -> mushroom stock or duxelles
button-mushroom.storageMethod: Refrigerate 34-40F in a paper bag or the original carton in the main compartment, not the crisper; do NOT seal in plastic or wash until use — trapped moisture makes them slimy.
button-mushroom.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (fresh whole mushrooms 4-7 days, sliced 3-5 days) and Penn State Extension (Agaricus bisporus grown indoors year-round; button, cremini, portobello are the same species at different maturities)
button-mushroom.depthNote: Buy whole over sliced — you nearly double the hold-life and can steer the trim into stock or duxelles.

cabbage.cutSpec: Whole green head, outer leaves + stem end trimmed, core shredded in (USDA FBG raw chopped/shredded). Core removed + heavy trim drops toward ~0.64.

lamb-shoulder.cutSpec: Bone-in lamb shoulder; boned & trimmed usable meat

lamb-shoulder.trimToValue: bones -> lamb stock; trim -> grind for kofta, merguez, or lamb burgers

lamb-shoulder.peakSeason: spring — traditional 'spring lamb' eats best from early spring to early summer
lamb-shoulder.depthSource: USDA FSIS 'Lamb From Farm to Table' / AskUSDA — fresh lamb roasts/chops 3-5 days refrigerated at <=40F; American Lamb Board (lamb quality) + USDA 'spring lamb' definition for the traditional spring-to-early-summer eating peak (lamb is available year-round)
lamb-shoulder.depthNote: Shoulder out-braises leg every time — buy it for your slow lamb dishes and grind the trim for merguez.

leek.yieldSource: White-and-light-green reference band ~0.44 (US Foods/USDA) to ~0.52 (The Book of Yields); 0.50 midpoint. Freezer 8-12 mo blanched-allium band (NCHFP/extension).

leek.trimToValue: dark green leek tops -> stock (too fibrous to eat, ideal for stock)

leek.peakSeason: fall through winter, sweeter after frost
leek.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (leeks ~1-2 weeks refrigerated) + USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide (cool-season crop)
leek.depthNote: Never toss the dark green tops — bag them for stock; that's roughly a third of the leek's weight you already paid for.

leg-of-lamb.cutSpec: Bone-in leg of lamb; boned & trimmed usable meat
leg-of-lamb.yieldSource: Butcher-test yield (lamb leg boned & trimmed ~68%); USDA Nutrient Data Set for Retail Lamb Cuts (roasted ~25% loss, ~0.75); USDA/FSIS FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart (fresh lamb 4-12 mo).
leg-of-lamb.yieldNote: A bone-in leg gives ~0.70 usable meat and loses ~25% roasted, so buy about 3/4 lb raw per bone-in portion to land a 4-5 oz plate.

leg-of-lamb.peakSeason: spring — traditional 'spring lamb' eats best from early spring to early summer
leg-of-lamb.depthSource: USDA FSIS 'Lamb From Farm to Table' / AskUSDA — fresh lamb roasts/chops 3-5 days refrigerated at <=40F; American Lamb Board (lamb quality) + USDA 'spring lamb' definition for the traditional spring-to-early-summer eating peak (lamb is available year-round)
leg-of-lamb.depthNote: Buy lamb in spring for best eating quality; bones and trim off a whole leg make stock and kofta grind.

lemon.cutSpec: whole fruit, reamed for juice (zest is a separate yield); juice yield ~0.35-0.45
lemon.yieldSource: Univ. extension citrus single-strength juice ~45% of weight; per-fruit math ~2-3 Tbsp per 100-115 g lemon (0.38-0.44); USDA Ag. Handbook 102; NCHFP freezing-citrus-juice 4-6 mo.
lemon.yieldNote: A lemon gives ~40% of its weight as juice (~1.5 fl oz); if your press runs lower the fruit is cold or under-ripe, so bring to room temp and roll firmly before pressing.

lemon.trimToValue: peels/zest -> oleo-saccharum, preserved lemons, candied peel, or lemon oil; juiced halves -> deglazing and board/pan cleaning
lemon.storageMethod: Refrigerate in the crisper ~40F (about 3-4 weeks) — far longer than the counter's ~1 week; keep dry and do NOT bag airtight.
lemon.peakSeason: winter through spring (Dec-May) for peak juice and flavor; available year-round
lemon.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS): lemons refrigerated 3-4 weeks; USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide + UC citrus guides — California harvests essentially year-round with a winter-spring quality peak.
lemon.depthNote: The fridge triples a lemon's life versus the counter — buy the case, hold cold, and always zest before you juice so nothing is wasted.

lime.cutSpec: whole fruit, hand-pressed/reamed for juice (real juice yield spans ~0.25-0.42 by fruit/season)
lime.yieldSource: USDA Ag. Handbook 102 (Food Yields) citrus juice yields + USDA FoodData Central; culinary juice charts (Weigh School ~0.22-0.28, bar rule ~0.42, ~4-5 fl oz/lb); NCHFP (Univ. of Georgia) freezing-citrus-juice best quality 4-6 mo.
lime.yieldNote: Budget ~a third of a lime's weight as juice (real yield runs 0.25-0.42); price fresh-lime drinks off juice-per-case, not per-fruit, and freeze surplus juice (~4 mo) instead of eating spoilage.

substitutes.name: lemon (juice + zest)

lime.trimToValue: peels/zest -> oleo-saccharum, candied peel, or citrus-oil finishing zest; juiced shells -> infused simple syrup
lime.storageMethod: Refrigerate loose in the crisper ~40F (roughly 3-4 weeks) or up to a week at cool room temp; do NOT seal airtight (trapped moisture -> mold), and juice/zest before the skins dry out.
lime.peakSeason: year-round (imported); freshest, most affordable supply late spring through summer
lime.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS/foodsafety.gov): citrus refrigerated ~3-4 weeks; limes are imported year-round (mostly Mexico, USDA AMS) so there is no US domestic in-season window.
lime.depthNote: Limes are steady year-round, so juice and freeze in cubes when a case lands cheap; a whole lime gives more juice at room temp or after a 10-second roll under your palm.

mango.yieldSource: National Mango Board ~0.69 and US Foods (per USDA Ag. Handbook 102) 'without pit & skin' 69% — two sources agree ~0.68-0.69; variety spread ~0.60-0.70+; NCHFP frozen-fruit 8-12 mo.
mango.yieldNote: Expect ~2/3 usable after skin and pit; firm Tommy Atkins runs lower than Ataulfo, so weigh a test case before you lock a portion size or a per-plate cost.

mango.storageMethod: Ripen on the counter until it gives to gentle pressure, THEN refrigerate 5-7 days; do NOT fridge hard/unripe mangoes (chill injury stalls ripening).
mango.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS): ripe mango ~1 week refrigerated (5-7 days); imported year-round (Mexico Mar-Sep leads), so no meaningful US domestic in-season window, with a May-Sep quality peak.
mango.depthNote: Buy mangoes firm and ripen on your own counter to control the flow — never fridge them hard, or they stall and never sweeten.

masa-harina.yieldSource: Finished dry-flour convention (fully usable, no trim, shelf-stable so not freezer-dependent); ~2.4x hydration from Masienda milled-masa guidance and the standard masa-harina-to-water dough ratio.
masa-harina.yieldNote: Reach for masa harina over fresh masa when turnover is low: 1 lb of dry flour hydrates to roughly 2.4 lb of dough and stores dry on the shelf for months, so you carry no daily masa spoilage.

substitutes.name: fresh masa (masa preparada / prepared nixtamal dough)
substitutes.ratio: 1:1 (use ready dough in place of masa harina you'd rehydrate)

substitutes.worksFor: emergency thickening or rustic corn dough when nothing else is on hand

masa-harina.storageMethod: Store the dry flour airtight in a cool, dry, dark pantry (68-72F), sealed against humidity and pantry pests; do NOT refrigerate the dry bag (invites condensation) — freeze for holds beyond ~1 year, and once hydrated into masa use the dough within a day or two
masa-harina.peakSeason: Year-round shelf-stable; best used within ~9-12 months of milling
masa-harina.depthSource: Culinary/producer consensus (Masienda, U. of Maine Extension): dry masa harina 9-12 mo pantry; fresh/hydrated masa 2-3 days refrigerated (shelfLifeDays 2 = conservative fridge life of prepared dough)
masa-harina.depthNote: One bag of masa harina is your on-demand tortilla/tamal/sope line — mix only what a shift needs, since hydrated masa won't keep

mint.cutSpec: leaves + tender tips; woody lower stems discarded (leaves-only ~0.50)
mint.yieldSource: Leaves-only cited ~0.50 (meez); 0.70 only if tender tips are kept, a prep-dependent estimate with no independently verified per-item table. Not citrus (juice null); raw use (cooked null); no sourced freeze figure (null).
mint.yieldNote: A plated sprig uses it all, but leaf-picked mint for tea or tabbouleh can drop toward half the bunch, so weigh picked leaves and expect roughly 0.5-0.7 depending on how much tender tip you keep.

mint.trimToValue: mint stems -> steep into tea, simple syrup, or infused water
mint.storageMethod: Refrigerate 34-40F, stems in water with tops loosely bagged, or wrapped in a damp towel; do NOT store dry-sealed — mint wilts and blackens quickly.
mint.depthSource: UC Davis Postharvest Center (fresh culinary herbs; tender-herb hold ~1-2 weeks) and extension harvest guidance (perennial mints peak before flowering); available year-round via greenhouse, hence empty domestic in-season array
mint.depthNote: Treat mint like basil's hardier cousin — water at the stems, and reroute trim into house tea or syrup instead of the bin.

mozzarella.peakSeason: year-round (fresh mozzarella eats best within a day or two of its make date)
mozzarella.depthSource: Does It Go Bad? fresh-mozzarella storage guide — opened fresh mozzarella keeps ~4-7 days (up to ~1 week submerged in refreshed water/brine) (https://www.doesitgobad.com/how-to-store-fresh-mozzarella/).
mozzarella.depthNote: Order fresh mozz to a 4-5 day turn and refresh its water; if a batch is aging, pivot it to cooked apps rather than the caprese board.

mussels.cutSpec: live in-shell → steamed shucked meat (after culling non-openers)
mussels.yieldSource: FAO 'Processing Mussels, Cockles and Whelks' (meat ~8-20% of whole; blue mussel ~20% meat-to-live; plump cultivated to ~30%); FDA Cold Food Storage Chart (shucked mussels 3-4 mo).
mussels.yieldNote: Only ~a quarter to a third of in-shell mussels is meat (thin/spawning lower, plump cultivated higher), and you'll cull non-openers — buy about 1 lb in-shell per appetizer.

mussels.storageMethod: Store live in a breathable bowl/mesh under a damp cloth at 35-40F; do NOT seal airtight or hold in fresh water (kills them) — best cooked within a day or two; discard any that won't close
mussels.peakSeason: Fall through early spring — cooler months, when farmed mussels are plumpest
mussels.depthSource: Washington State Dept. of Health shellfish handling (live mussels 3-4 days); FDA 'Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely'
mussels.depthNote: Rope-farmed mussels are cheap, sustainable, and year-round — the plumpest ones come in the cooler months, and the pot liquor is free broth.

napa-cabbage.cutSpec: Whole napa head, base + a few outer leaves trimmed (USDA FBG untrimmed → ready-to-serve raw). Freeze only blanched, for cooked use.

napa-cabbage.yieldNote: Napa is ~0.93 usable — almost no trim — so it's often the cheapest slaw or stir-fry green per usable pound.

napa-cabbage.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper/FoodSafety.gov and storage refs (whole napa ~1-2 weeks, cut 3-5 days) + extension cool-season guides (fall-dominant crop, secondary spring crop).
napa-cabbage.depthNote: Slaw, stir-fry, or kimchi from one head — more tender than Western cabbage and it still holds about two weeks whole.

octopus.cutSpec: whole → cleaned (beak, ink sac, viscera, eyes removed); then braise

octopus.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper / FDA (1-2 day fresh cephalopod hold); Monterey Bay Seafood Watch (octopus largely imported, sold frozen year-round — no meaningful US domestic season)
octopus.depthNote: Buy it frozen on purpose — the freeze tenderizes it, so you get a better braise for less money and less risk.

okra.cutSpec: Stem caps trimmed; pods used whole or sliced (USDA 14% refuse).
okra.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central refuse ~14% (okra, raw — stem caps) → 0.86. Freeze: NCHFP (blanch whole pods).
okra.yieldNote: ~0.86 after trimming the caps — cost cleanly, and freeze blanched pods when local summer okra is cheap to carry the price through winter.

okra.depthSource: University extension storage guides (okra best in ~2-3 days, chilling-sensitive); USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide for season
okra.depthNote: Okra is a 2-3 day buy — order it tight to service in high summer, and lean on file or a dark roux when you need the thickening without the pod.

Olive oil is a shelf-stable pantry item (unopened ~18-24 mo from harvest; opened EVOO best within ~1-3 mo).
olive-oil.yieldNote: Heat, light, and air kill olive oil -- not room temperature -- so store it sealed in a cool, dark spot off the line and do not refrigerate or freeze; opened EVOO fades in flavor within 1-3 months, so buy finishing oil in sizes you will actually use.

olive-oil.depthNote: Buy on the pressed/harvest date, not the best-by; the freshest crop lands late fall, and your finishing EVOO should be a different SKU from your line frying oil.

onion.yieldNote: Budget ~1.14 lb whole yellow onion for every 1 lb you need peeled and diced; freeze diced trim for cooked apps only, best within ~8 months as texture softens.

onion.trimToValue: onion skins and root trim -> stock (adds color and savory depth)
onion.storageMethod: Hold cool (50-60F), dry, dark, and airy in mesh or open crates; do NOT refrigerate whole onions and do NOT store next to potatoes — each speeds the other's spoiling.
onion.peakSeason: late summer to fall (storage onions); available year-round from storage
onion.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper storage times (foodsafety.gov: onions ~1 month pantry) + USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide (snaped.fns.usda.gov)
onion.depthNote: Dry-store onions in ventilated crates, not the walk-in — cold softens them and their odor taints nearby produce.

oyster-mushroom.depthNote: The most delicate of the bunch — order close to service, keep them dry in paper, and cook within a few days.

parmesan.yieldSource: StillTasty (FSIS-based): frozen Parmesan block holds best quality ~12-18 months (12 = conservative pick), grated ~8-18 months; MasterClass storage guide. edibleYield ~0.95 is a small-trim estimate (rind is a few percent of a wedge and reusable in stock).

parmesan.trimToValue: parmesan rinds -> simmer into soups, stocks, risotto, and tomato sauce for umami (fish them out before serving)
parmesan.storageMethod: Refrigerate at 34-40F wrapped first in parchment/wax paper then loosely in foil or a container so it can breathe, re-wrapping after each use. Do NOT seal wet or in airtight plastic alone (traps moisture and invites surface mold).
parmesan.depthSource: MasterClass, 'How to Store Parmesan Cheese' — opened wedge keeps ~1-2 months refrigerated, wrapped in parchment then foil to breathe (https://www.masterclass.com/articles/how-to-store-parmesan-cheese); 45 days is the mid-range operator value.
parmesan.depthNote: A parm wedge outlasts almost anything in your walk-in — buy the whole piece over pre-grated, grate to order, and bank the rinds for stock.

parsley.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (fresh herbs) and UC Davis Postharvest Center — parsley among the most durable tender herbs, holding ~2 weeks refrigerated; hardy and available year-round
parsley.depthNote: The most forgiving herb in your walk-in: about two weeks of hold, and every stem earns its keep in stock or chimichurri.

parsnip.cutSpec: topped and peeled; woody core removed only on large old roots
parsnip.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central parsnip refuse ~15% (edible ~0.85) + Chefs Resources 85%; freezer up to 12 mo blanched (NCHFP/extension parsnip guidance).

parsnip.depthNote: Menu parsnips after the first frost — cold is what turns them sweet, so a fall-winter special eats better and buys cheaper.

pear.yieldSource: US Foods (per USDA Ag. Handbook 102) 'without pit & skin' = peeled & cored = 78%; USDA FoodData Central refuse ~8-10% skin-on (cored-only ~0.90); NCHFP frozen-fruit 8-12 mo. (spec corrected: 0.78 is the peeled-AND-cored value, not cored skin-on).
pear.yieldNote: Peeled-and-cored pears run ~78% usable; leave the skin on (cored only, ~0.90) where the plate allows and buy to the trimmed weight, not the whole fruit.

pear.trimToValue: peels + cores -> simmered syrup, jelly, or poaching liquid (cores are pectin-rich)

pear.depthNote: Pears ripen from the inside out — buy firm and check the neck by the stem; a soft belly means it's already mealy at the core.

pineapple.cutSpec: peeled, light trim, core often left in (~0.50); a strict eyes-out + cored trim per USDA AH-102 drops to ~0.38
pineapple.yieldSource: USDA FoodData Central pineapple refuse ~49% (edible ~0.51) + Book of Yields via Chefs Resources ~0.50-0.53; USDA Ag. Handbook 102 / US Foods list a heavier eyes-out+cored trim at 0.38; NCHFP frozen-fruit 8-12 mo.
pineapple.yieldNote: About half a whole pineapple is usable flesh (less if you cut the eyes deep and core it out, ~0.38), so a $3 pineapple is really ~$6/lb of flesh; buy pre-cut only when it beats that true cost.

substitutes.failsFor: dishes needing pineapple's bright acidity; papaya is milder and softer

pineapple.trimToValue: core + skins -> tepache (fermented pineapple drink), simmered syrup, or juice
pineapple.storageMethod: Hold whole at cool room temp 1-2 days, then refrigerate (about 5-7 days); refrigerate cut pineapple covered and use within 5-7 days — do NOT leave cut fruit at room temp.
pineapple.depthSource: USDA FoodKeeper (FSIS): pineapple whole ripe / cut refrigerated 5-7 days; US supply is imported year-round (Costa Rica ~80%+), so no US domestic month window, with a Mar-Jul quality peak.
pineapple.depthNote: Pineapple does not sweeten after cutting — buy fragrant and heavy-for-size, hold whole a day or two, then break it down to order.

pork-belly.depthNote: Air-dry the skin uncovered in the fridge overnight before roasting — that's the difference between crackling and rubber.

pork-loin.cutSpec: Boneless pork loin; surface fat & silverskin trimmed
pork-loin.yieldSource: Culinary boneless-loin trim references (~0.85); USDA retail cooking-yield reference (roasted ~0.75); USDA/FSIS FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart (fresh pork 4-12 mo).

pork-shoulder.depthSource: USDA AskUSDA 'How long can you store pork' / FSIS — fresh pork roasts 3-5 days refrigerated at <=40F; corroborated by FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart, FDA Refrigerator & Freezer Storage Chart, and Clemson HGIC 'Safe Handling of Pork'

portobello-mushroom.cutSpec: cap, woody stem removed; gills-in ~0.85, gills scraped ~0.75

whole-chicken.storageMethod: Refrigerate at 40F or below on the bottom shelf in a leak-proof tray/bag; use within 1-2 days or freeze. Do NOT wash raw poultry (splashing spreads bacteria) and do NOT let juices drip onto ready-to-eat foods.
whole-chicken.depthSource: USDA FoodSafety.gov Cold Food Storage Chart and USDA FSIS 'Chicken from Farm to Table': raw whole poultry keeps 1-2 days refrigerated at 40F; broiler chicken is farmed continuously (non-seasonal). FDA Refrigerator & Freezer Storage Chart agrees.
whole-chicken.depthNote: Two days max on the raw bird, then freeze or cook -- and bank every carcass and wingtip into stock so the whole-bird buy carries a second yield.

whole-crab.cutSpec: whole hard-shell blue crab (Callinectes) → hand-picked meat
whole-crab.yieldSource: US Foods 'Common Product Yields' (blue 17%, Dungeness 27%, king 25% from shell) + Chesapeake hand-pick references (~14-15%, ~2.25 oz/lb); FDA Cold Food Storage Chart (cooked shellfish 3 mo).
whole-crab.yieldNote: DMV blue crab hand-picks at only ~15-17% meat — that's why picked crab costs what it does; Dungeness/king run ~25-27% if a recipe allows a swap.

whole-crab.depthSource: Maryland DNR Chesapeake blue crab season (Apr 1-Dec 15); FDA & WA State DOH shellfish handling (cook live crab day of purchase; store under a damp cloth, never submerged)
whole-crab.depthNote: Blue crab is your local Chesapeake edge — hard-shell is heaviest in the fall, soft-shell peaks late spring, and the shells make a bisque.

whole-lobster.depthSource: Maine DMR / Maine Lobster Marketing Collaborative (peak late June-early Dec); FDA & WA State DOH shellfish handling (cook live lobster day of purchase; store under a damp cloth, never in fresh water)

whole-salmon.cutSpec: whole dressed (H&G, gutted head-on) → boneless, pin-boned, belly/brown-fat-trimmed fillet
whole-salmon.yieldSource: Chefs Resources & Reluctant Gourmet fish-fillet yield charts (H&G salmon → skin-on fillet 68-72%, ~60% after full pin-bone/belly/brown-fat trim); FDA Cold Food Storage Chart (fatty fish 2-3 mo); fish cooking-loss references (~15-20%).

whole-salmon.depthNote: Wild whole salmon in summer buys you frames and collars for staff-meal stock plus a gravlax program off one fish — break it down in-house; farmed Atlantic covers you year-round.

whole-turkey.cutSpec: Whole bird; edibleYield 0.50 is the practical planning yield of cooked pickable meat off the carcass (bone + skin removed), industry range ~40-50%. cookedYield 0.70 is the roast shrink of the intact bird (cooked whole / raw whole) — a separate measure, do not multiply the two.
